title: Next Generation of Ultra-Coarse-Graining: Self-Consistent Inference of Critical Internal States
authors: Weizhi Xue, Xiao Shuai, Gregory A. Voth
abstract: Bottom-up coarse-graining expands the length and time scales accessible to molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, but information loss can hinder accurate representation of multistate phenomena in complex biomolecular dynamics. Ultra-Coarse-Graining (UCG) projects discrete "quantum-like" extended degrees of freedom, or "internal states," onto coarse-grained (CG) molecules, extending CG model expressiveness. The rapid-local-equilibrium (RLE) approximation in UCG depends on user-defined collective variables (CVs, e.g., local density) and neglects correlations between internal states within and between CG molecules. We present Self-Consistent UCG (SC-UCG), which uses the underlying UCG interactions directly to assign internal states without designing CVs in the CG ensemble. During simulation, internal state probabilities are determined self-consistently through graph message passing. We enhance the RLE Hamiltonian with the Bethe approximation and AI-based inference to represent explicit correlations between UCG beads. For force-field training, we develop Multilayer Internal State Consistency (MISC), a machine-learning method derived from relative entropy minimization that avoids iterative sampling of intermediate force fields. We apply SC-UCG to a tetramer exhibiting a second-order symmetry-breaking phase transition from a supercritical racemic fluid to subcritical D-rich and L-rich fluids. SC-UCG captures collective switching of internal states in the subcritical region and recapitulates the phase transition across temperatures, despite being trained on a single-temperature dataset.
summary: This work introduces Self-Consistent Ultra-Coarse-Graining (SC-UCG) to improve molecular simulations by accurately handling complex internal states. It bypasses the need for manually defined collective variables by deriving state probabilities self-consistently using graph neural networks trained via relative entropy minimization. This allows for robust simulation of phase transitions in systems like biomolecular tetramers.
main_problem: The primary challenge is overcoming information loss during coarse-graining (CG) that prevents accurate sampling of complex, multistate phenomena in molecular dynamics simulations.
main_result: The proposed Self-Consistent UCG (SC-UCG) method successfully captures collective switching of internal states and accurately reproduces phase transitions even when trained on data from a single temperature.
method: It introduces SC-UCG, which self-consistently infers internal state probabilities using graph message passing derived from minimizing relative entropy. The training utilizes the Multilayer Internal State Consistency (MISC) framework via graph backpropagation.
model_or_system: The method is applied to a model tetramer system exhibiting a second-order symmetry-breaking phase transition between supercritical racemic and subcritical D/L-rich fluid phases.
key_observables: Internal state probabilities, collective switching events, and the order parameter characterizing the phase transition.
important_parameters: Temperature (T), coupling strengths derived from UCG interactions, and the structure of the internal states.
main_assumptions: The core approximation is that the system can be modeled as a mixed ensemble where internal state probabilities are determined self-consistently without relying on pre-defined collective variables (CVs).
figures_summary: Not specified in the notes, but the application demonstrates capturing phase transitions and state switching.
paper_structure: The paper builds from foundational bottom-up CG theory to introduce SC-UCG as an advancement over RLE approximations. It details the variational derivation leading to a message-passing form (ISC layer) for internal state inference, followed by training via MISC and application to phase transition simulations.
why_interesting: The self-consistent treatment of discrete 'internal states' within a continuum framework is highly relevant for modeling quantum or near-quantum degrees of freedom in condensed matter systems where simple mean-field approximations fail.
